passages.t: The sword of the LORD comes down on Edom
passages.happening:
‘Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples’ (verse 1). The LORD is angry with all the nations and their armies; he has devoted them to destruction (verse 2). Verse 3 pictures the slain left unburied on the mountains.

‘All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll’ (verse 4), and the stars will fall like withered leaves from a vine.

Then the sword comes down on Edom, the people devoted to destruction (verse 5). ‘The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood’ (verse 6). ‘For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom’ (verse 6). ‘For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 34 and 35 form a pair that closes the poetry of the book's first half before the narratives of chapters 36 to 39. They set two destinies side by side: a land turned to wilderness, and a wilderness turned into a garden.

Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Its people traced their descent to Esau, Jacob's brother, and the two nations had a long history of hostility, from Edom's refusal to let Israel pass through its land to its wars with the kings of Judah. Edom was remembered with special bitterness because it gloated over and took part in the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC. Bozrah, probably modern Buseirah in southern Jordan, was one of its chief cities.

When these chapters were written is debated. The traditional view assigns them to Isaiah in the eighth century as prophecy. Many critical scholars date them to the exile or later, because Edom's betrayal in 587 or 586 seems to lie behind them and because chapter 35 is so close to chapters 40 to 66; some speak of the two chapters as a bridge joining the book's halves. On any view, Edom here stands for more than one small nation: it represents every power that sets itself against God and his people.

The language of sacrifice and the rolled-up sky is the poetry of judgment, drawn from ancient war and worship. It is not a report of a single battle.
passages.later: Obadiah condemns Edom for its part in Jerusalem's fall: ‘Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame’ (Obadiah 1:10). Revelation uses verse 4's picture: ‘The sky receded like a scroll being rolled up’ (Revelation 6:14).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand a chapter that pictures God's sword bathed in blood and a whole nation devoted to destruction?

The chapter is poetry of judgment, full of deliberate exaggeration and stock pictures drawn from ancient war and sacrifice, not a description of a single battle. Its first readers heard it as the vindication of victims: Edom had helped destroy Jerusalem, and the chapter assured the powerless that God would not ignore injustice. The language of sacrifice presents judgment as belonging to God alone, not as permission for human vengeance. Elsewhere Scripture forbids God's people to take revenge themselves: ‘Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge’ (Leviticus 19:18), and ‘Do not avenge yourselves’ (Romans 12:19).

Readers still differ on how to hold these texts. Some stress that Edom here is a symbol of every power opposed to God, so that the chapter is about the final defeat of evil. Others stress the historical Edom, and note that the region did become desolate and its people absorbed into others. Many Christians also read such chapters in light of the cross, where God's judgment on sin is borne by God himself.

These notes name no people or nation of the present day as Edom. The chapter gives no one a warrant to wish destruction on any people, or to carry it out.
passages.asks: The chapter assures victims that God has a day of recompense for their cause. Ask what wrong done to you, or to others, you need to leave in God's hands rather than avenge. And ask what it would mean to trust that God sees every injustice.

passages.t: A land returned to chaos, and the scroll of the LORD
passages.happening:
Edom's streams will be turned to tar and its soil to sulfur; its land will become blazing pitch (verse 9). It will not be quenched, day or night. ‘Its smoke will ascend forever’ (verse 10). No one will pass through it again.

The desert owl, the screech owl, the great owl and the raven will live there. ‘The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction’ (verse 11). No nobles will be left to proclaim a king (verse 12). Thorns and thistles will grow over its towers, and it will be a haunt for jackals and ostriches (verse 13). Desert creatures and hyenas will meet there, and the night creature will find rest (verse 14). The owl will nest and the birds of prey gather (verse 15).

‘Search and read the scroll of the LORD: Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate, because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit’ (verse 16). He has given them the land as their portion forever (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The burning pitch and sulfur recall the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, which lay not far from Edom's land. The measuring line of chaos and the plumb line of destruction are builders' tools used in reverse. God measures Edom out not to build but to unbuild, laying out a ruin.

The wild creatures who take over the land are a familiar picture of a ruined city in the ancient world. The night creature of verse 14 translates the Hebrew lilit, related to Mesopotamian names for female demons of the night; later Jewish legend built stories of a demon called Lilith around the word. The BSB renders it simply as a creature of the night.

Edom declined in the following centuries. By the later Persian period Arab peoples, and afterward the Nabataeans, controlled its homeland, and many Edomites moved into southern Judah, which came to be called Idumea.

Verse 16 invites the reader to check the scroll. Every creature God named will be there. His word will not fail.
passages.later: Malachi looks back on the same land: ‘I have made his mountains a wasteland and left his inheritance to the desert jackals’ (Malachi 1:3). The next chapter turns the wilderness the other way: ‘The wilderness and the land will be glad’ (Isaiah 35:1).
passages.asks: Verse 16 invites the reader to search the scroll and see that God's word has not failed. Ask what promise of God you could search out and test. And ask what the reversal from chapter 34 to chapter 35 says about the God who judges and restores.
